newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korean peninsula in turmoil over defection, scandal.
newsitem.headline: Korean peninsula in turmoil over defection, scandal.

text.p: One of Pyongyang's top ideologues on Wednesday became the highest ranking North Korean to seek asylum in the South, but the government in Seoul had little time to gloat as it slid further into disarray over a loans scandal.

Hwang Jang-yop, 73, a senior advisor to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il and one of 11 secretaries on the powerful secretariat of the Workers' Party, sought asylum in Seoul's Beijing embassy along with an aide, officials in Seoul said.
The defection revealed cracks in the country's Stalinist hierarchy and was widely seen as a blow to Kim four days before his heralded 55th birthday celebrations.

"Workers' Party secretary Hwang Jang-yop expressed his intention to defect at 10:05 a.m. (0205 GMT) at the consular section of the embassy," Ryu Kwang-sok, director-general of the Foreign Ministry's Asia-Pacific Bureau, told reporters.
But North Korea's de facto embassy in Japan, the General Association of Korean Residents in Japan, denied the reports and said Hwang was due to return to Pyongyang on Thursday.

O Huyong-jin, General Association Vice Chairman, said Hwang and three other North Korean officials took a train that left Beijing on Wednesday afternoon and were due to cross the border into North Korea at around noon on Thursday.
"We confirmed with the North Korean embassy in Beijing, as well as back home (in Pyongyang), that Secretary Hwang left Beijing for Pyongyang," O Huyong-jin told reporters in Tokyo.

Hwang is credited with developing the quirky theory of Juche, a brand of fanatic self-reliance on which former "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung built his personality cult and challenged capitalist South Korea in a Cold War confrontation.
In Seoul, President Kim Young-sam faced his own political challenge as a loans scandal involving the failed Hanbo Steel Co claimed its first cabinet victim, one of the president's most trusted aides.
Home Affairs Minister Kim Woo-suk offered his resignation hours before prosecutors began grilling him on whether he took kickbacks to secure loans for Hanbo.
Hanbo Steel managed to wring $6 billion of loans from the financial system when it had a net worth of just $300 million.

Another Kim Young-sam lieutenant, Hwang Byung-tai, was also questioned by prosecutors as a probe into what is shaping up as South Korea's biggest corporate scandal further eroded the president's credibility.
Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung made known he was ready to resign to try to take responsibility for the scandal and limit damage to the government.
Prosecutors have already arrested another close associate of the president along with the third ranking member of the ruling New Korea Party.

Kim Young-sam, whose reputation was built as an anti-corruption crusader, cannot run for a second term in presidential elections in December but is widely thought to be seeking a successor to preserve his influence.
With scandal swirling around his inner sanctum, analysts said his ability to set the political aganda was waning.

The South Korean Foreign Ministry said Seoul was now seeking Beijing's cooperation in allowing the defector safe passage to Seoul. China is one of North Korea's few friends and backed Pyongyang in the 1950-53 Korean War.
An armistice that ended one of the most brutal conflicts in history sealed the division of the Korean peninsula into communist North and capitalist South.

The defection is a major coup for Seoul, although South Korea is nervous of any sign that North Korea may be collapsing. The country is on the brink of famine and there are fears it could lash out at Seoul with its million-strong army and chemical weapons if it crumbled.
"Hwang's defection is the strongest ever signal the Stalinist regime's hierarchy is cracking," said Park Hun-ok, senior fellow at Seoul's privately-funded Institute of North Korean Studies.
He is also a member of the party's central committee and is in charge of its foreign policy, according to Seoul officials who rank him number 24 in the Pyongyang power structure.
Sunday's birthday celebrations are widely seen as part of an image-boosting effort intended to pave the way for Kim Jong-il's formal accession to power this year.
